title: Build for Survival
realOrConstructed: Constructed challenge in a historically grounded setting
bigUnderstanding: Shelter is an engineering tradeoff: speed, weather protection, stability, fire safety, labor, scarce imported materials, and repairability. There is no single right design. Early Jamestown builders used local wood and clay (mud-and-stud, daub, thatch) because it was fast and local, but it needed constant maintenance in Virginia weather.
winCondition: Design shelter for about 105 people, including 15 families with children, that is fast, dry, stable, safe and buildable with what you have. Then survive the tests and fix whatever breaks.

opening.intro:
Spring, on the coast of Virginia. Your ships have just dropped anchor in a wide, brown river. Behind the muddy shore: thick forest, marsh grass taller than you, and clouds of mosquitoes. About 105 tired people are standing on the bank with their bags: soldiers and workmen, a few gentlemen, and 15 families with 25 children, from babies to 14-year-olds. Every one of them needs a roof before the storms and cold nights come.

You can't ship houses across an ocean, so you'll build with what's here. Design shelter that's fast, dry, stable, safe from fire, and buildable with your people and tools. Then test it, and fix whatever fails.

cards.label: Your targets
cards.text: FAST · DRY · STABLE · SAFE (fire!) · BUILDABLE · REPAIRABLE. Homes for about 105 people (25 are children), plus a way to cook, latrines, storage and water. 30 builders, 6 kegs of nails.

cards.label: What's around you
cards.text: Forest, young saplings, clay-rich mud, marsh reeds and grasses, dirt, and oyster shells along the shore.

cards.label: The place
cards.text: Hot, sticky summers. Hard rain and storms. Cold nights later in the year. Low, damp ground near the river.

cards.label: Carpenter
cards.text: We can cut trees, but every beam takes work. Nails are precious. I know ways to join wood with pegs instead.

cards.label: Quartermaster
cards.text: We've got axes, saws, hammers, shovels, rope, a few kegs of nails, and some old sail canvas. Hardly any boards, bricks or glass.

cards.label: Settlement leader
cards.text: Every person building is a person not fishing, farming or standing guard. We also need somewhere dry for food and tools.

cards.label: A mother of three
cards.text: My children can't sleep in a room with fifty strangers. We need our own space, a safe fire to cook on, and somewhere dry for the baby.

opening.prompt: What do you want to know, or what are you thinking of building?

facilitatorNotes: Monica's design notes: the problem is NOT 'draw a house.' Abi balances speed, weather, stability, fire, labor, scarce nails, repairability and housing many people.

WHO'S HERE (constructed): the real first Jamestown group (1607) was all men and boys; English women and families came from 1608 on, and the 1587 Roanoke colony included families. Families change the design: privacy (one big barracks with families and single men together will cause real trouble), each family wanting its own hearth (more fires = more fire risk), children near hearths, babies needing warm dry beds, and more roofs and walls. Let Abi weigh it; don't tell her the answer.
Never show the toolbox as a menu. If she asks what's possible, describe a few techniques briefly, not prices.

Engineering tradeoffs to judge by: one big barracks is fast and shares walls, but crowds people and one fire or failure hits everyone. Many small buildings isolate fire and failure but need more roofs and labor. Nails simplify joints but are scarce. Daub uses local stuff but needs labor and upkeep. Thatch is local and light but burns and needs repair.
Abi's mom is an architect; Abi may know some building terms. Don't assume she does; don't over-explain either.

End reveal: archaeologists at Jamestown found early colonists built with local wood and clay using mud-and-stud construction. Daub mixed clay with plant fibers, and early roofs could be thatch. Fast, local, but high-maintenance in Virginia weather. The real fort burned in January 1608. Make clear her settlement, design and tests were constructed.
justInTimeConcepts: Post-in-ground: posts set straight into holes; fast, but the buried wood rots.
Stud and lath: small upright pieces and thin strips that hold the wall filling.
Daub: clay mixed with grass or straw, pressed onto lath; dries hard but washes away if it stays wet.
Thatch: bundled reeds or straw laid thick on a steep roof so rain runs off.
Bracing: diagonal pieces that stop a frame from leaning over in wind.
Load: the weight and push (like wind) a structure has to carry.
scaffolds: Follow a raindrop from the sky to the ground. Where does it go on your building?
If one building catches fire, what else goes with it?
What will need fixing after a few months, and what will you fix it with?
completion: A valid design that shelters at least 105 people within the labor and nail limits; every stress test passed with her final design (testing runs straight through; any failure means a redesign and retest); then her answer to 'Would you approve this shelter system for the settlement's first year? Why?'

endReveal.concept: Engineering tradeoffs: every design choice buys something and costs something. Early Jamestown used mud-and-stud buildings: fast and local, but they needed constant upkeep.

vocabulary.meaning: Clay mixed with plant fibers, used to fill walls.
A roof of tightly bundled reeds or straw.
Diagonal pieces that keep a frame from tipping.
Getting one benefit by giving up another.

realVsConstructed.real: Early colonial Virginia's climate and materials, mud-and-stud construction, daub, thatch, scarce nails, and the fire that burned Jamestown's fort in January 1608. English women and families came to Jamestown from 1608 on, and the 1587 Roanoke colony included families.
realVsConstructed.constructed: Your settlement and who's in it (the real first Jamestown group was all men and boys), its exact numbers, the labor and nail budgets, and the sequence of tests.

targets.label: FAST
targets.check: Enough shelter before exposure becomes dangerous (roughly within 3 weeks).

targets.label: DRY
targets.check: People and supplies stay reasonably dry, from rain and from damp ground. Babies and small children get sick fast in damp beds.

targets.label: SAFE
targets.check: Manages fire and crowding risks, especially where children sleep near hearths.

targets.label: BUILDABLE
targets.check: Fits the labor, tools and materials available.

targets.label: REPAIRABLE
targets.check: Settlers can maintain it with what they have, without waiting for England.

existingResources: About 105 settlers: about 50 single men (soldiers, laborers, a few gentlemen) and 15 families (15 couples, 25 children from babies to 14). Roughly 30 adults can build at once; the rest fish, farm, guard, cook and care for children
Clay-rich soil, earth, marsh reeds and grasses, oyster shell
Axes, saws, hammers, digging tools, rope
6 kegs of iron nails (scarce: no more until a supply ship)
Old sail canvas: enough to cover about 8 building sections, temporarily
Very few imported boards; almost no brick or glass
environment: Hot, humid summers; colder nights later in the year.
Heavy rain and occasional strong storms.
Low, damp ground near the river.

buildingBlocks.name: Roof
buildingBlocks.examples: what keeps the rain out overhead

buildingBlocks.name: Layout

toolbox.name: Post-in-ground frame section, pegged joints (about 10×16 ft, sleeps 5)
toolbox.provides: Posts set in holes, studs and beams joined with wooden pegs. No nails, more work.
toolbox.maintenance: Buried post ends rot in damp ground within a few years.

toolbox.name: Post-in-ground frame section, nailed joints (about 10×16 ft, sleeps 5)
toolbox.provides: Same frame, joined with nails: faster, uses scarce nails.
toolbox.maintenance: Buried post ends rot in damp ground within a few years.

toolbox.name: Daub walls, one section (clay + grass pressed onto lath)
toolbox.provides: Solid, warm walls from local clay. Takes work to mix and press.
toolbox.maintenance: Cracks and washes out if rain hits it for long; patch with fresh clay.

toolbox.name: Woven-stick walls only, no clay, one section
toolbox.provides: Quick woven sapling walls. Drafty and lets in blowing rain.

toolbox.name: Board walls, one section (imported boards)
toolbox.provides: Fast, tight walls, but only enough boards for about 6 sections.

toolbox.name: Bark-slab walls, one section
toolbox.provides: Peeled bark slabs tied or pegged to the frame.
toolbox.maintenance: Bark curls and splits; needs replacing.

toolbox.name: Thatched roof, one section (marsh reed)
toolbox.provides: Thick reed bundles. Sheds rain well on a steep roof. Burns easily.
toolbox.maintenance: Patch every season; birds and wind pull it apart.

toolbox.name: Bark-covered roof, one section
toolbox.provides: Overlapping bark slabs. Less likely than thatch to catch a spark.
toolbox.maintenance: Slabs crack and shift; replace some each season.

toolbox.name: Sail-canvas roof, one section
toolbox.provides: Very fast. Only enough canvas for about 8 sections.
toolbox.maintenance: Rots and tears within a few months.

toolbox.name: Board roof, one section (imported boards)
toolbox.provides: Tight roof, but boards are almost gone.

toolbox.name: Quick lean-to (branches and brush, sleeps 4)
toolbox.provides: Up in an hour. Leaks, blows apart in storms.

toolbox.name: Dug well
toolbox.provides: A well dug inside the settlement and lined with timber. Enough water for about 150 people.

toolbox.name: Pit latrine
toolbox.provides: A dug pit with a simple screen around it. Serves about 20 people.

toolbox.name: Open hearth (fire pit)
toolbox.provides: A ring of stones for a cooking and heating fire, inside or beside a building. Cooks for one family (about 4 people).

toolbox.name: Storehouse section for food and tools
toolbox.provides: A frame, walls and roof section for supplies (sleeps no one). Holds food, tools and powder for about 60 people.

toolbox.name: Raised floor or sleeping platforms, one section
toolbox.provides: A wooden floor built up off the ground on short posts.

toolbox.name: Drainage ditch around one building
toolbox.provides: Ditches dug around and between buildings.

toolbox.name: Deep overhanging eaves, one section
toolbox.provides: Roof edges built to stick out past the walls.

toolbox.name: Diagonal bracing, one section
toolbox.provides: Diagonal braces added to the frame.

toolbox.name: Clay-lined chimney or fire hood, one building
toolbox.provides: A clay-lined chimney over a hearth. Cooks for one family (about 4 people).

toolbox.name: Separate outdoor cookhouse
toolbox.provides: A small separate building with a big hearth. Cooks for about 35 people.

toolbox.name: Fire spacing and water buckets
toolbox.provides: Cleared gaps between buildings, buckets of water and a person on watch.

toolbox.name: Bent-sapling house section covered in bark or reed mats (sleeps 5)
toolbox.provides: Powhatan-style: saplings bent into arches, covered with mats or bark. Sheds rain; easy to repair.

measurements.label: Check the ground where you'd build
measurements.result: Near the river it's low and squishy, with puddles after rain. A little higher ground sits about 100 yards back, firmer and drier.

measurements.label: Test the local clay
measurements.result: Sticky, good clay. Mixed with chopped grass it dries hard in a few days of sun. Pure clay cracks as it dries.

measurements.label: Check the marsh reeds
measurements.result: Tall, tough reeds in big stands. Plenty for roofs if people cut and bundle them, which is slow work.

measurements.label: Look at the trees nearby
measurements.result: Lots of straight young trees good for posts and studs, and big oaks and pines that take a long time to cut and move.

measurements.label: Ask about storms
measurements.result: Locals warn that late-summer storms bring winds strong enough to flatten weak shelters and drop dead branches.

measurements.label: Count the nails
measurements.result: 6 kegs. That's it until a supply ship comes, maybe months away.

measurements.label: Ask how many people can build
measurements.result: About 30 at a time. The rest must fish, farm, gather and guard, or people go hungry.

measurements.label: Ask the families what they need
measurements.result: They want their own space, even if small. Each family wants a hearth to cook on and to keep warm at night. Parents worry about little ones near fires and in damp beds. Several mothers say they'd happily help build, plaster walls and thatch if someone watches the children.

stressTests.name: Heavy rain
stressTests.passesIf: Check roof shedding and leaks, wall erosion (daub washes out if walls stay wet), ground drainage, stored food and tools, damp sleeping areas. Credit drainage, steep roofs, overhangs, raised floors or storage, higher ground. Check where the babies and small children sleep: damp, cold beds make them sick fast.

checks.label: Something that sheds rain and keeps water away (drainage ditches, eaves/overhangs, or raised floors)

stressTests.name: Wind and storm
stressTests.passesIf: Check how posts are anchored, how roofs are attached, big flat walls or roofs catching wind, nearby trees that could fall, and bracing. Lean-tos and canvas roofs fare badly.

stressTests.name: Fire
stressTests.scenario: At night, a spark escapes from a cooking or heating fire.
stressTests.passesIf: Check thatch and wood exposure, spacing between buildings, where hearths are, whether there's water and a plan, and whether one fire could destroy all shelter and stores. A well-designed settlement may lose one building, not everything. Check where children sleep relative to hearths and whether families have a safe place to cook. Many family hearths means many chances for a spark.

checks.label: A plan to keep one fire from spreading (clay chimneys, a separate cookhouse, or a firebreak between buildings)

stressTests.name: Labor and time
stressTests.scenario: Food work is falling behind because too many people are still building or repairing.
stressTests.passesIf: Check total work, number of buildings, dependence on scarce nails or boards, build speed and maintenance burden. Designs near the labor limit or heavy on upkeep struggle. Separate family houses mean more roofs and walls; one big barracks is faster but causes privacy fights and spreads sickness and fire.

stressTests.name: Maintenance
stressTests.scenario: After months of weather, some daub has cracked and washed out, thatch needs patching, and wood touching the ground is going soft.
stressTests.passesIf: Passes if repairs can be done locally with what they have (clay, reeds, timber), without waiting for England. Designs that depend on nails, boards or canvas struggle.

data.designFor: About 105 people: about 50 single men plus 15 families (15 couples and 25 children, from babies to 14-year-olds).
